paragraphs: Natural gradient has an attractive geometric property: changing the coordinates used to describe a model should not change its optimization behavior. However, this invariance holds for infinitesimally small updates. Practical algorithms take finite steps, so different parameterizations can produce different optimization trajectories even when they describe the same underlying model.

The paper studies this mismatch through Riemannian geometry and numerical methods for differential equations. It defines an order of invariance according to how quickly a numerical method approaches an invariant solution. Higher-order integrators and geodesic corrections then provide ways to make finite-step trajectories better preserve the intended geometry. The authors prove numerical convergence properties for the corrected updates and show that they can be as computationally efficient as ordinary natural-gradient updates.

Experiments cover deep neural network training and natural policy gradient in reinforcement learning. In these settings, the proposed techniques improve optimization speed over traditional natural gradient. The findings connect a theoretical property of optimization trajectories with practical training benefits, while retaining the distinction between exact infinitesimal invariance and its numerical approximation.
icml-2018-accelerating-natural-gradient-.tldr: Higher-order integration and geometric corrections make practical natural-gradient updates more invariant and improve optimization speed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Options let a reinforcement-learning agent organize sequences of decisions into larger behavioral units. This form of abstraction can support decisions in complex environments, but specifying the options by hand creates additional work and limits scalability. The paper addresses how an agent can learn these units directly through interaction.

The authors introduce a policy-gradient method that uses inference to improve all available options simultaneously. Learning does not require observed labels identifying which option generated each part of the experience. The method can also operate off-policy, allowing learning from experience without requiring that it come from the policy currently being improved. Its differentiable inference procedure is reported to produce options that are easy to interpret.

The empirical results support these properties and indicate better sample efficiency than existing methods for learning options end to end. The contribution therefore connects automatic behavioral abstraction with more effective use of interaction data. Its reported advantage concerns learning useful, interpretable options without supplying option labels, rather than assuming that the agent's higher-level behaviors have already been designed.
icml-2018-an-inference-based-policy-grad.tldr: An inference-based policy-gradient method learns interpretable options without option labels and shows improved sample efficiency.

paragraphs: A collection of already-trained prediction models can offer different balances between accuracy and computational expense. This paper presents an approximation algorithm that turns such a collection into a cascade. The resulting predictor retains similar accuracy while reducing the average cost of making predictions, making model selection part of how the system processes its inputs.

The automatically constructed cascades exhibit behavior that gives a concrete explanation for the savings. Easier images can be handled using lower-resolution inputs. Computationally cheaper models also face higher confidence requirements, so low cost alone is insufficient to justify accepting their predictions. These properties connect the amount of computation used to the apparent difficulty of the particular image and the confidence of the model handling it.

Applied to ImageNet classification models, the approach achieves reductions of up to twofold in floating-point multiplications and up to sixfold in average memory input/output. These are reported upper-end improvements, and the cost objective is explicitly average-case. The findings show how coordinating existing predictors can improve inference efficiency while preserving similar predictive accuracy.
icml-2018-approximation-algorithms-for-c.tldr: An algorithm assembles pretrained models into cascades that retain similar accuracy while lowering average prediction cost.

paragraphs: The paper develops a parallel optimization method for nonconvex problems, where the objective can have multiple competing solutions. Its starting point is theory showing that stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can support local and global convergence guarantees under certain conditions. The authors use this foundation to construct an asynchronous stochastic L-BFGS algorithm.

The method supports both distributed machines and workers sharing memory. Asynchronous operation allows parallel work without requiring every worker to proceed through synchronized rounds. The theoretical analysis establishes an ergodic convergence rate of O(1/√N), where N is the total number of iterations. It also shows that linear speedup is possible under certain conditions; this is a conditional scaling result, rather than an unconditional promise about adding workers.

Experiments use synthetic and real datasets. Their results support the analysis and show a significant speed advantage over a recently proposed synchronous distributed L-BFGS algorithm. Together, the theory and experiments make the case that asynchronous execution can accelerate this form of nonconvex optimization while retaining a formally analyzed convergence behavior.
icml-2018-asynchronous-stochastic-quasi-.tldr: An asynchronous stochastic L-BFGS method offers analyzed convergence, conditional linear speedup, and empirical gains over a synchronous alternative.

paragraphs: The problem is to identify which available action, or arm, has the largest expected reward. The setting assumes that every arm's mean reward depends linearly on the same unknown d-dimensional parameter vector. Learning this shared vector provides a way to reason about the arms together, rather than treating every expected reward as an unrelated quantity.

The authors design a randomized estimator of the unknown vector using a convex relaxation of an optimal G-allocation experimental-design problem. This links estimation to the choice of informative observations. From that estimator, they develop one algorithm whose sample complexity depends linearly on the dimension d. A second algorithm has sample complexity that depends on reward gaps involving the best d arms.

The gap-dependent result matches the lower bound arising from ordinary top-arm identification. This places the result against a fundamental sample requirement, rather than only against another algorithm's performance. The paper also compares its methods empirically with existing algorithms on sample complexity and computation time. The abstract reports these comparisons without claiming a particular empirical winner.
icml-2018-best-arm-identification-in-lin.tldr: Experimental-design-based estimation yields linear-bandit best-arm algorithms with linear dimension dependence and a reward-gap-dependent sample guarantee.

paragraphs: Large studies often contain many experiments, each accompanied by descriptive variables. Analysis must determine which outcomes are statistically significant while managing false discoveries across the collection. Black Box FDR uses an empirical-Bayes approach to make these variables useful for discovery, learning predictive models that increase statistical power while controlling the false discovery rate.

The method divides analysis into two stages with distinct questions. First, a deep neural network supplies a prior used to identify experiments with significant outcomes. Second, separate black-box models for individual covariates help select variables with significant predictive power across experiments. This distinguishes finding noteworthy outcomes from identifying which recorded characteristics help explain variation in those outcomes.

The authors report that BB-FDR outperforms competing methods in benchmarks for both stages. In two studies of cancer drug efficacy, it discovers a larger proportion of significant outcomes and selects variables associated with key genomic drivers of sensitivity and resistance. These results support using flexible prediction within a framework that also addresses the statistical reliability of the selected discoveries.
icml-2018-black-box-fdr-74e8cc81fd.tldr: BB-FDR uses learned predictive models to identify significant experiments and informative covariates while controlling false discovery rates.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network requires a way to measure the difference between generated and real data distributions. The paper studies connections among three families of such measures: information-theoretic divergences, integral probability metrics, and Hilbert-space discrepancies. Understanding their relationships provides the theoretical foundation for a new training procedure called Chi-square GAN.

The proposed procedure is described as conceptually simple, stable during training, and resistant to mode collapse, the loss of diversity in generated outputs. Its formulation also extends naturally to matching several distributions simultaneously. This broadens the role of the method beyond a single comparison between one real distribution and one synthetic distribution.

The authors additionally reuse the trained critic through an importance-weighted resampling strategy that significantly improves sample quality. Thus, the critic contributes both to training and to the subsequent selection of samples. Across a range of generative-modeling tasks, experiments show improved stability and convergence alongside state-of-the-art results. Resistance to mode collapse is the stated claim, rather than a guarantee that collapse can never occur.
icml-2018-chi-square-generative-adversar.tldr: Chi-square GAN connects several distribution-matching criteria and combines stable training with critic-based resampling to improve generated samples.

paragraphs: A matrix network consists of multiple matrices connected by a weighted graph that describes their relationships. The paper asks how to complete such a network when observations are incomplete, including a sampling setting in which some matrices are entirely missing. Recovering those matrices requires using structure across the network, beyond the observed entries within any single matrix.

The central structural assumption is that the matrices have low rank after applying a graph Fourier transform across the network. This places the low-rank requirement in a representation informed by the relationships among matrices. Under the proposed framework, the authors formulate a convex optimization problem and prove an exact-recovery guarantee. The guarantee is tied to the structured recovery problem they define.

Numerical studies examine how rank and sampling rate affect exact recovery and reveal a phase-transition phenomenon. The paper also supplies an iterative imputation algorithm for efficiently solving the optimization problem at larger scales. Demonstrations include MRI and a Facebook user network, connecting the mathematical recovery framework to different kinds of linked matrix data.
icml-2018-convolutional-imputation-of-ma.tldr: A graph-based low-rank assumption enables convex recovery of partially observed matrix networks, including networks with entirely missing matrices.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label learning handles prediction problems with very large label collections, potentially exceeding one million labels. Tree methods help manage this scale by repeatedly dividing the overall problem into smaller subproblems. That organization can reduce both training and prediction costs and allows parts of the computation to run in parallel.

CRAFTML introduces a random-forest algorithm with a very fast partitioning procedure. The motivation is that leading tree approaches described in the paper use complicated partitioning strategies and do not exploit tree randomization. CRAFTML brings randomization into this setting while simplifying the partitioning work, targeting the computational burden of organizing a very large prediction problem.

Across nine datasets from the extreme multi-label literature, the reported comparisons favor CRAFTML over the other tree-based approaches. A parallel implementation using five cores is also competitive with leading methods run on hundred-core machines. This supports the method's practical efficiency in the reported evaluation. The comparison does not establish an exact hardware-normalized speedup, but it demonstrates competitive results with substantially fewer cores.
icml-2018-craftml-an-efficient-clusterin.tldr: CRAFTML combines randomized trees with fast partitioning to deliver competitive extreme multi-label learning using relatively few processing cores.

paragraphs: In decentralized training, different workers may collect data from different sources. Those datasets can contain useful differences, yet analyses of decentralized parallel stochastic gradient descent have relied on workers' data being sufficiently similar. This creates a mismatch between a desirable distributed-data setting and the assumptions supporting the training method.

D² addresses this issue by adding variance reduction to decentralized parallel stochastic gradient descent. The stated convergence-rate improvement removes the term involving variance across workers, leaving O(σ/√(nT)). The significance is specific: differences between workers' data no longer contribute the additional term appearing in the comparison rate. The paper uses this result to establish robustness to data variation across workers.

The empirical evaluation uses image classification with each worker restricted to data from a limited set of labels. That arrangement directly tests the kind of unequal local data access motivating the algorithm. D² significantly outperforms D-PSGD in these experiments. The theoretical and empirical findings therefore both support training when workers hold meaningfully different data.
icml-2018-d-2-decentralized-training-ove.tldr: D² adds variance reduction to decentralized training, improving its convergence rate and performance when workers hold different data.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process depends heavily on its kernel, which encodes the relationships the model uses to generalize from observations. Choosing an effective kernel can be difficult, especially when the data contain several interacting patterns. This paper introduces Neural Kernel Networks as a flexible, trainable representation of kernel structure.

The architecture follows valid kernel-composition rules, so every unit represents a valid kernel. This makes it possible to build complex kernels while preserving the mathematical requirements of the Gaussian-process model. The network can compactly approximate compositional structures of the kind used by the Automatic Statistician. Because the construction is differentiable, its parameters can be trained end to end using gradient-based optimization.

The authors establish universality for the class of stationary kernels, giving the representation a broad but explicitly scoped expressiveness result. Experiments demonstrate pattern discovery and extrapolation in time series and textures, along with applications to Bayesian optimization. These findings show how learning the kernel's composition can help a Gaussian process capture underlying structure that matters for predictions beyond observed data.
icml-2018-differentiable-compositional-k.tldr: Neural Kernel Networks learn valid compositional Gaussian-process kernels through gradient optimization and are universal within the stationary-kernel class.

paragraphs: Image restoration research often combines new network architectures with sophisticated losses or adversarial training. This paper investigates how far standard convolutional autoencoders can go when their architecture is chosen carefully. Its main result is that networks built from convolutional layers and skip connections can outperform the compared state-of-the-art restoration methods.

The key step is an evolutionary search for effective architectures. After selecting the architecture, training uses the ADAM optimizer to minimize an l2 reconstruction loss between restored images and their ground truth. The approach therefore puts the main design effort into finding a suitable network structure while keeping the stated training objective and building blocks simple.

The reported results are 27.8 dB PSNR on CelebA and 33.3 dB on SVHN, compared with 22.8 dB and 19.0 dB for the former leading methods, respectively. These findings demonstrate the strength of architecture search in the evaluated restoration settings. They support the claim that standard components can be highly effective, without establishing that adversarial training or more elaborate losses are unnecessary for every restoration problem.
icml-2018-exploiting-the-potential-of-st.tldr: Evolutionary architecture search produces standard convolutional autoencoders that outperform the compared image-restoration methods using simple reconstruction training.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation of high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models, which represent relationships among many variables. Graphical lasso is a popular approach, but the authors identify a statistical shortcoming: it does not achieve the oracle convergence rate. Their goal is to obtain that stronger estimation rate while keeping the computation tractable.

They formulate a nonconvex estimation problem and approximate it through a sequence of convex programs. This separates the desired statistical objective from the sequence of manageable optimization problems used to approach it. The proposed estimator achieves the oracle convergence rate. A contraction property characterizes the statistical error introduced by the sequential approximation, connecting the computational procedure to the accuracy of its output.

The methodology is also extended to semiparametric graphical models. Numerical studies report better estimation performance than other popular methods for Gaussian graphical models. The contribution combines an improved statistical guarantee with a practical route to computation: the convex approximations are analyzed as part of the estimator, rather than treated as an unrelated numerical convenience.
icml-2018-graphical-nonconvex-optimizati.tldr: Sequential convex approximations make a nonconvex graphical-model estimator tractable while achieving the oracle convergence rate.

paragraphs: Lloyd's heuristic for k-means repeatedly compares data points with cluster centers. These distance calculations can be expensive, with a major bottleneck arising from multiplying the data matrix by vectors representing centers. The paper targets this numerical operation by randomly sparsifying the original data matrix before clustering.

A sparse matrix permits faster matrix-vector multiplication, but the essential question is whether the modified data still support good clusters for the original data. The authors establish that an optimal k-means solution on the sparsified matrix gives an approximately optimal objective value on the original matrix. This is a guarantee about the optimal solution of the sparse problem; it does not turn Lloyd's heuristic into an exact optimizer.

Experiments on three real-world datasets support the theoretical findings and show satisfactory clustering performance. The practical appeal is that reducing the amount of matrix data involved in computation can accelerate an expensive step without significantly harming cluster quality. The paper thus links a numerical simplification to an explicit guarantee about the original clustering objective.
icml-2018-k-means-clustering-using-rando.tldr: Randomly sparsifying the data matrix speeds k-means computations while preserving an approximate-optimality connection to the original clustering problem.

paragraphs: Neural-network distillation typically trains a student to reproduce a teacher's output activations. Jacobian matching adds information about how those outputs change when the input changes. Matching this sensitivity can transfer aspects of the teacher's behavior beyond its output at a particular input, but choosing the matching loss has involved ad hoc decisions.

The paper provides a theoretical basis for that choice by establishing an equivalence between Jacobian matching and distillation with input noise. The authors use the connection to derive appropriate loss functions. They then extend the reasoning to transfer learning by showing that a recent transfer-learning procedure can be understood as distillation, making the same analysis relevant in that setting.

Experiments on standard image datasets show that Jacobian-based penalties improve distillation, robustness to noisy inputs, and transfer learning. These results support the usefulness of transferring input sensitivity alongside activations. The broader contribution is a connected explanation for the penalties: their design follows from an analyzed relationship with noisy-input training rather than relying solely on an arbitrary matching objective.
icml-2018-knowledge-transfer-with-jacobi.tldr: A connection between Jacobian matching and noisy-input distillation motivates losses that improve knowledge transfer and noise robustness.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks compact representations that preserve information useful for distinguishing classes. Many methods assume independent observations, but sequence data contain temporal relationships. LT-LDA addresses this mismatch by learning low-dimensional representations that account for the structure of entire sequences rather than treating their observations as independent examples.

The method uses temporal alignments to establish sequence structure and builds class separability around those structures. Crucially, an alignment may change when the representation changes. The authors therefore learn the subspace and its associated alignments together, optimizing an objective that favors temporal structures that are easy to distinguish across classes. This joint treatment makes the representation and the sequence comparisons part of the same learning problem.

The paper connects the objective to alignment inference, which enables an iterative solution. It provides theoretical insight and evaluations on real-world sequence datasets to support the approach. The stated contribution is a way to make dimensionality reduction sensitive to temporal organization, while allowing that organization to adapt as the lower-dimensional representation is learned.
icml-2018-learning-low-dimensional-tempo.tldr: LT-LDA jointly learns a compact representation and temporal alignments to make sequence classes easier to distinguish.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning commonly treats learning the dynamics and learning the reward function as separate problems. A flawed dynamics model complicates that separation: it can produce states that never occur in the real environment. The reward model must still assign values to those imagined states when they appear in model-generated experience.

The paper introduces an error bound that explicitly accounts for the reward model's behavior on states sampled from the learned model. This makes reward prediction on model-generated states part of the performance analysis. The authors use the bound to extend Hallucinated DAgger-MC, an algorithm with theoretical performance guarantees for deterministic Markov decision processes that do not require a perfect dynamics model to be learnable.

Empirically, the resulting approach to reward learning can dramatically improve control when the dynamics model is flawed. The result highlights an interaction between two learned components: a reward function must be useful within the imperfect model that supplies its inputs. The stated theoretical setting is deterministic MDPs, and the large control improvements are empirical possibilities.
icml-2018-learning-the-reward-function-f.tldr: Accounting for rewards on states generated by an imperfect dynamics model can substantially improve model-based control.

paragraphs: Photometric stereo estimates the orientations of a three-dimensional surface from images taken under different lighting conditions. Unknown reflectance properties make this difficult because image appearance depends on both surface orientation and how the material reflects light. Learning-based approaches also face the difficulty of obtaining accurate surface-normal labels for training.

The paper proposes a convolutional network within a physics-based, unsupervised framework. The network predicts surface normals and reflectance functions, then feeds those predictions into the rendering equation to synthesize the observed images. Its weights are optimized during testing by minimizing the discrepancy between those synthesized images and the actual observations. The observed images themselves therefore provide the reconstruction objective used to fit the network.

This procedure requires neither ground-truth normals nor pretraining on external images. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on a challenging real-world scene benchmark. The result shows how an image-formation model can provide a useful learning signal for recovering surface properties, even when directly supervised training data are unavailable and the surfaces have general, unknown reflectance.
icml-2018-neural-inverse-rendering-for-g.tldr: A physics-based network recovers surface normals and reflectance by reconstructing observed images, without normal labels or external pretraining.

paragraphs: Understanding a demonstration can require recovering the decision logic behind the visible behavior. This paper targets that goal through neural program synthesis: the model produces an explicit underlying program from demonstration videos. The videos can be visually complicated and can show different behaviors, so successful synthesis requires integrating more than a single uniform sequence of observations.

The proposed model includes a summarizer module designed to combine information from multiple behaviorally diverse demonstrations. This addresses how evidence from different executions can contribute to the inferred program. The authors also use a multi-task training objective to encourage meaningful intermediate representations while training the system end to end. These two design choices support both combining demonstrations and organizing the information learned from them.

The reported results show reliable synthesis of underlying programs and capture of the diverse behaviors present in demonstrations. The contribution is therefore an explicit route from visual examples to programmatic decision logic. It connects interpretation of observed behavior with a structured output that represents the program behind that behavior.
icml-2018-neural-program-synthesis-from-.tldr: A neural synthesizer integrates diverse demonstration videos to recover explicit programs using a summarizer and multi-task training.

paragraphs: Tracking multiple particles through noisy images becomes ambiguous when nearby particles overlap or look identical. A single chosen set of tracks hides that ambiguity, but exact Bayesian inference is computationally intractable in this setting. The paper develops an approximate Bayesian approach that retains uncertainty about both particle positions and identities.

The method uses a neural network to approximate the filter-backward-sample-forward inference algorithm. Its amortized design learns an inference procedure that can then be applied to tracking data. By changing the simulated data used to train the network, the approach can handle a wide variety of data types. This makes simulation a means of adapting the inference system to different particle-tracking settings.

The authors report improved accuracy over the state of the art while also producing uncertainty estimates. At test time, runtime scales linearly with data length and with the number of particles, supporting application to very large datasets. The central benefit is that preserving ambiguity need not require the poor scaling of previous approximate Bayesian methods or the information loss of a single best-track estimate.
icml-2018-scalable-approximate-bayesian-.tldr: A simulation-trained neural inference method tracks particles with uncertainty estimates and linear test-time scaling.

paragraphs: Sequential optimization can require every tested decision to satisfy safety constraints, even when both utility and safety are initially unknown. StageOpt addresses this problem using Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization. It accommodates feedback that gives an absolute utility value or expresses a preference, broadening the forms of observation that can guide the search.

The algorithm separates two activities into distinct stages: expanding the region regarded as safe and maximizing utility. Existing approaches described in the paper interleave those activities. StageOpt's separation makes the search more efficient and naturally applicable to a broader class of problems, according to the authors. They also provide theoretical guarantees for satisfying safety constraints and converging to the optimal utility value.

Evaluation includes synthetic experiments and clinical use for spinal cord stimulation therapy. The reported results show greater effectiveness than existing safe-optimization approaches and safe, effective optimization in the clinical experiments. These findings connect the algorithm's organization with an application where the quality of intermediate decisions matters as well as the final utility achieved.
icml-2018-stagewise-safe-bayesian-optimi.tldr: StageOpt separates safe-region expansion from utility maximization and provides safety and convergence guarantees alongside successful clinical experiments.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning controllers use a generic multilayer perceptron for the nonvisual part of their policy. Structured Control Nets introduce a simple architectural division: one module is nonlinear and the other is linear. The intended roles are complementary, with nonlinear control handling broader, forward-looking behavior and linear control stabilizing local dynamics around the remaining residual.

The authors hypothesize that this structure can combine the advantages of linear and nonlinear policies. Their desired benefits include better sample efficiency, final reward, and generalization with a smaller network and compatibility across training methods. They evaluate the hypothesis in MuJoCo, Roboschool, Atari, and a custom urban-driving simulation, using multiple black-box and policy-gradient methods together with ablation and generalization tests.

The reported results are competitive and support the proposed architecture. A locomotion case study further shapes the nonlinear module to emulate biological central pattern generators and achieves much improved performance. This illustrates how control-specific prior knowledge can be built into the architecture. Broader improvements from such priors are presented as potential, rather than an established result for every control task.
icml-2018-structured-control-nets-for-de.tldr: Structured Control Nets combine linear and nonlinear policy modules, with competitive control results and gains from locomotion-specific structure.

paragraphs: Complex demonstrations can contain smaller behaviors that are useful across several tasks. Learning reusable policies for those behaviors makes it possible to pool their training examples and compose them into new tasks. The challenge is determining where each behavior occurs without requiring detailed temporal labels or domain-specific knowledge.

TACO uses task sketches that specify only the order of subtasks in each demonstration. It jointly aligns those sketches with the observed sequence and learns the corresponding sub-policies. Consequently, identifying the boundaries and learning the behaviors inform one another. The authors report that this joint procedure generalizes better than optimizing the alignment and policy-learning problems separately.

The evaluation spans multiple domains, including a simulated three-dimensional robot arm controlled from images alone. The reported performance is comparable to fully supervised approaches while requiring substantially less annotation. The result supports a useful middle ground in learning from demonstrations: the learner receives the intended subtask sequence, but it works out how that sequence lines up with the observed actions while learning to perform them.
icml-2018-taco-learning-task-decompositi.tldr: TACO jointly aligns ordered task sketches with demonstrations and learns reusable sub-policies, achieving comparable performance with less annotation.

paragraphs: Speech synthesis must capture how words are delivered as well as which words are spoken. This paper extends Tacotron so that a reference recording can supply the desired prosody. The system learns a latent embedding from an acoustic representation of that reference, then conditions speech generation on the learned embedding.

The authors show that synthesized speech can follow the reference prosody in fine temporal detail even when the reference speaker and the synthesis speaker differ. This means that the transferred delivery is not restricted to reproducing the same speaker. They also demonstrate synthesis of text different from the reference utterance, showing that a reference embedding can be reused beyond its original words.

The evaluation introduces quantitative and subjective measures of prosody transfer and includes audio examples from single-speaker and 44-speaker Tacotron models. Together, these results support using a learned reference representation to guide expressive speech synthesis across changes in speaker and text. The contribution is a mechanism for transferring aspects of delivery through a learned conditioning space.
icml-2018-towards-end-to-end-prosody-tra.tldr: A reference-derived prosody embedding lets Tacotron transfer expressive delivery across speakers and to different text.

paragraphs: Visual control needs representations that make goals meaningful and support planning toward them. Universal Planning Networks learn such representations by embedding differentiable planning inside a goal-directed policy. A forward model unfolds possible behavior in a latent space, and gradient-based trajectory optimization searches for an action plan within that representation.

The planning process and the representation are trained together using a supervised imitation-learning objective. This ties the learned space directly to the task of producing useful plans from demonstrations. The authors find that the resulting representations also provide a distance measure for goals expressed as images. That distance can define rewards for model-free reinforcement learning aimed at reaching new target states.

Using those image-goal rewards substantially improves learning on new tasks in the reported experiments. The authors also demonstrate successful transfer of visuomotor planning strategies between robots with substantially different shapes and actuation capabilities. These findings show that a representation learned through planning can remain useful beyond its original imitation task, supporting both new goal-directed learning and transfer across different robot bodies.
icml-2018-universal-planning-networks-le.tldr: Universal Planning Networks learn visual representations through differentiable planning that also support new image-goal tasks and transfer across robots.
